b: The knockout stage of the Total Chess Pilot began in Budapest on Tuesday, with Alireza Firouzja and Anish Giri winning the opening sets of their semifinal matches against Fabiano Caruana and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, respectively. The day also saw Magnus Carlsen attract attention for a different reason: having already secured victory against Bibisara Assaubayeva, the Norwegian decided not to play the final fast classic game, which he lost by forfeit.

Following Monday's rest day, all 24 participants returned to action. The tournament's unusual format keeps every player in contention, although only the four group winners can still compete for the overall title. The remaining participants are divided into five additional knockout brackets, according to their finishing positions in the group stage. The six brackets, each featuring four players, will determine the final standings, with the second-placed players competing for fifth place, the third-placed players for ninth place, and so on.

Each knockout match consists of two sets, played on consecutive days. A set features four blitz games, worth 1 point per win; two rapid games, worth 4 points per win; and one fast classic game, worth 8 points per win. The scores reset after each day, meaning that winning the first set by a large margin provides no advantage beyond the result itself.

The format has raised a few questions, particularly regarding the order of play. Why begin with blitz rather than the longer time control, as is often the case in mixed-format competitions? Should the players not be encouraged to show their best chess in the longest game, rather than reaching it already tired after six faster encounters?

The scoring system is another point of discussion. A rapid victory is worth four times as much as a blitz win, meaning that a player who loses all four blitz games can equalise the score with a single rapid victory. This was precisely what happened in Tuesday's match between Firouzja and Caruana in the main bracket.

It remains to be seen whether the organisers will address these questions ahead of the 2027 Total Chess Tour. After all, the tour will award two of the eight places (i.e. 25 percent) in the Candidates Tournament.
Playing seven games against elite opposition is surely exhausting - Ian Nepomniachtchi v. Jan-Krzysztof Duda and Haik Martirosyan v. Richard Rapport | Photos: Michal Walusza
Firouzja and Giri take the lead

The four group winners are competing for the overall title, with Firouzja facing Caruana and Giri taking on Vachier-Lagrave in the semifinals. Both Firouzja and Giri won their opening sets on Tuesday, though their victories came in rather different circumstances.

Firouzja defeated Caruana by a 12–8 score, making full use of his speed in the blitz section. The Frenchman won all four games to take a 4–0 lead, but saw his advantage disappear immediately when Caruana won the first rapid encounter, worth 4 points.

The American then had good chances to score a second consecutive victory in the following game, which would have given him the lead. However, Firouzja managed to turn things around in a hard-fought encounter, showing his quickness once again during the time-trouble phase. Thus, his ability to handle the faster time controls proved crucial.

With the two players having exchanged rapid victories, the score stood at 8–4 in Firouzja's favour ahead of the fast classic game. A draw in that final encounter left the Frenchman with a 12–8 victory in the opening set.
Alireza Firouzja (winner) v. Fabiano Caruana | Photos: Michal Walusza

Giri's victory over Vachier-Lagrave was more straightforward, despite five of the seven games ending in draws. The Dutchman won one blitz game, while the remaining three blitz encounters and both rapid games were drawn. The decisive result came in the fast classic encounter, in which Vachier-Lagrave was already in a must-win situation.
Giri won that game as well, securing a 14½–5½ victory. Although most of the games ended peacefully, the Dutchman appeared to be in better shape throughout the day.

Neither Caruana nor Vachier-Lagrave is out of contention, however. Under the regulations, winning Wednesday's second set by any margin would force an Armageddon decider. The combined scores of the two sets would only determine the choice of colour in case that sudden-death game takes place.

In the knockout for fifth place, Hans Niemann and Ian Nepomniachtchi recorded clear victories over Le Quang Liem and Jan-Krzysztof Duda, respectively. Both winners scored with the white pieces in their fast classic encounters, collecting 8 points from the most valuable game of the day.
The matches in the bracket for ninth place were more closely contested, with Arjun Erigaisi getting the better of Jorden van Foreest and Haik Martirosyan defeating Richard Rapport.

Elsewhere, Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and Wesley So won their opening sets in the knockout for 13th place, while Magnus Carlsen and Vladislav Artemiev did the same in the bracket for 17th place. Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Abhimanyu Mishra were the winners in the knockout for 21st place.
Jorden van Foreest was defeated by Arjun Erigaisi | Photo: Michal Walusza
Shakhriyar Mamedyarov beat Levon Aronian in the battle of veterans | Photo: Michal Walusza
Carlsen forfeits final game against Assaubayeva

One of Tuesday's main talking points was Carlsen's decision not to play the final fast classic game against Bibisara Assaubayeva. The Norwegian had already secured victory in their opening set, having collected three wins and a draw in blitz, followed by two rapid victories. The score stood at 11½–½, leaving Assaubayeva unable to catch up even with the 8 points available in the final game.

Carlsen, however, had an additional consideration. His difficult group-stage performance had cost him 21.8 classical rating points, leaving him on 2801.2 in the live rankings, just above the 2800 mark. A draw against Assaubayeva would have taken him below 2800 for the first time in 17 years, while a defeat would have left him just 0.7 points ahead of Hikaru Nakamura. A Caruana victory could also have ended his uninterrupted reign as world number one, which began in July 2011.
Bibisara Assaubayeva played six rapid and blitz games against Magnus Carlsen on Tuesday | Photo: Michal Walusza

As it happened, the game was never played. Assaubayeva waited at the board, and after 15 minutes Carlsen was given a forfeit loss. Speaking to Norway's TV 2, the Norwegian explained that the match already decided and believed that, if the final game still had to be played, it should not count towards the ratings.

That position is not unheard of in match situations where the result has already been decided. However, it subsequently became clear that the organisers had informed the players during the pre-event technical meeting that all games would be played and rated.

Total Chess founder Kjell Madland explained that, with the match already decided, Carlsen did not need to play the final game. Madland also stated that no changes had been made to the regulations, implying that other players in the same situation would be able to make the same decision without facing consequences.
The incident prompted criticism on social media. Emil Sutovsky wrote:
Hard to comment on such a pathetic unsportsmanlike conduct.

Hans Niemann published a longer statement questioning whether the regulations were being applied consistently while bringing back past situations in which he considered that Carlsen had been favoured by organisers:

Whether games could count even after the match was discussed and agreed upon in the technical meeting. If Carlsen was playing someone with a higher rating, he might have been more inclined to play. Nevertheless, if any other player forfeited a game, disrespecting the organiser and his opponent, they would have lost the match by forfeit. It's incredibly disappointing to see continued favouritism towards one player. Let's not forget the jeans, and "Co World Champion" saga. All rules must be applied equally, regardless of the player. End of story.
Wesley So, on the other hand, took a more understanding view of Carlsen's decision, pointing to the rating implications:
He has nothing to gain. If he draws, Hikaru will be very happy! Hikaru's just like a crocodile waiting on the water right now.
